newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkey puffs on despite public smoking ban.
newsitem.headline: Turkey puffs on despite public smoking ban.

text.p: Turks lit up in taxis, buses and cramped offices in defiance of new restrictions on smoking in public, a habit that borders on a national pastime.
"It doesn't make any difference to me," said Faruk Uzeltepe, dragging on a cigarette in a badly-aired public notary office.
He was breaking the law introduced by the Islamist-led government on Tuesday that forbids smoking in public buildings, workplaces with six or more employees and on public transport.
A notary clerk puffed away on a strong Turkish brand cigarette despite a no-smoking sign on the once-white bare wall, now a yellowish hue after years of exposure to smoke.

Under the law, offenders face fines of 10 million lira ($100) if they do not stub out after a warning. Bus drivers and the managers of buildings where smoking is restricted must pay the same amount if they do not enforce the ban.

"Nobody's going to do anything about it. There are so many laws in Turkey that go unheeded anyway," said Uzeltepe, an administrator at a local chamber of commerce. He coughed and sniffed from a winter cold.
The poorly-paid consumer protection police, stretched to the limit controlling minor fraud and tax evasion by small shopkeepers, are to be the arbitrers of the smoking ban.
Smoking is much more socially acceptable in Turkey than in the West.
Non-smoking households often display a tray of foreign and Turkish cigarettes to offer guests. Diners at restaurants will almost never complain about others lighting up between courses.
No-smoking signs and a separate area for smokers were absent from Ankara's busy main post office on Tuesday in a breach of the new law.
"Of course, go ahead," said a counter attendant when asked if smoking was allowed.
Battered by annual inflation of around 80 percent and restraints on freedom of expression, many Turks say tobacco is one of the few vices left to them.
A packet of 20 of Turkey's cheapest cigarettes costs only 30,000 lira ($0.36)
"The Turkish people have too much stress and the media gives too much space to cigarette advertising," said Selahhatin Kaptanoglu, head of the Green Crescent anti-tobacco group.
He said 22 million of the country's 60 million people use the weed.

"They should do something about heroin gangs and the rest of the filth before they touch smokers," said the notary clerk in reference to a scandal over alleged links between a convicted drug smuggler and the police force.
Tobacco is a major source of income in western Turkey's Aegean coastal region where government subsidies to growers are perennial vote winners.
Turkey produced 200,000 tonnes of tobacco last year for the large domestic market and for export to be blended with the U.S-grown crop.
